content.title: THE {{KITCHEN MISTAKES}} MOST PEOPLE ARE STILL MAKING
facts: **Chicken** – Washing it in the sink before cooking (splashes bacteria like Campylobacter onto counters, sponges, and utensils).
**Melon** – Leaving cut cantaloupe or honeydew out on the counter for hours (moist, low-acid flesh lets Listeria and Salmonella multiply fast).
**Leftover pasta** – Cooling it slowly on the stove instead of the fridge (Bacillus cereus spores can survive cooking and grow at room temp).
**Eggs** – Storing them in the fridge door instead of the main shelves (door temps swing every time it opens, speeding up bacterial growth).
**Garlic-in-oil** – Making a jar and keeping it at room temperature (low-oxygen environment is a known risk for Clostridium botulinum).
**Ground beef** – Judging doneness by color alone instead of using a thermometer (pink meat can be safe and brown meat can still be undercooked).
**Berries** – Rinsing them right after buying instead of right before eating (extra moisture speeds up mold growth in the fridge).
**Canned goods** – Ignoring a bulging or dented can because it 'still smells fine' (a swollen lid can signal gas from harmful bacteria growth).

content.caption:
A few of these are easy to overlook. Chicken feels 'cleaner' after a rinse, but that quick splash under the tap can send bacteria-laden water droplets up to three feet across your sink and counters, landing on anything nearby. Leftover pasta is another sneaky one — letting a big pot cool slowly on the stove keeps it in the temperature danger zone for too long, giving Bacillus cereus spores (which can survive the original cooking) time to multiply before you even put it away. And that homemade garlic-in-oil trend? Garlic stored in oil at room temperature creates exactly the low-oxygen, low-acid conditions Clostridium botulinum needs to grow, which is why it should always be refrigerated and used quickly. Everyone's kitchen habits are a little different, so it's worth double-checking your own routine against these.
